column121: Vectored to join the Rwy XX ILS inside ZZZZZ; called the field and cleared for the visual. Disconnected to autopilot to descend and join the glide slope (which was below us). Continued to hand fly since the Aircraft wouldn't lock the glide slope outside the localizer. As localizer came in; the flight directors remained on the horizon and unusable. I asked the FO (First Officer) to turn off and turn on both flight directors to regain their use. At that point (just outside ZZZZZ1) the flight directors were giving us good glide slope and localizer information. We put the gear down and commenced to slow to approach speed inside ZZZZZ1 (still hand flying) and I disconnected the autothrottles somewhere around 1000 ft. AGL. Approximately 600 ft. (inside 3 miles) we received an aural 'Glide Slope; Glide Slope' warning. At that time I noticed that while my flight director in the HUD and on the PFD was centered; the glide slope information was deflected all the way to the top of my display. A quick scan of the FO's PFD showed centered flight director as well. Checking the PAPIs for Rwy XX showed 4 red. I leveled off and added power to fly to the glide slope again; readjusted power; and landed uneventfully. No warnings or cautions were displayed.When we reconnected the Flight Directors inside ZZZZZ; descending on the glide slope; they came back directly where I wanted them showing me on glide slope and on course. I did not check LOC and glideslope annunciations on the PFD. Is it possible they did not capture the glideslope? I would doubt that since I got a Glideslope aural warning. I have no idea why the flight directors both sides had us descending below glide slope inside 3 miles on the approach. Wrote [a maintenance] entry; called [maintenance control] and conferenced in the Avionics tech for a verbal debrief on the gripe.I guess I could have caught the error had I been cross checking the glide slope on the right hand side of the HUD display; but I sit back far enough that I have to make an effort to see it; and it's not in my habit pattern on a visual. I'm normally working lineup; glide slope; airspeed; and any crosswind correction looking outside and through the HUD. It was my error for not scanning the PAPI to detect the gradual settle - which I'll put down to fatigue - but the flight director was centered! Long day. Error captured and uneventful landing - but very troubling to see the flight directors do that.
column123: On visual approach to ZZZ Rwy XX; we were GS/LOC captured; on speed with the AP off. I was looking outside when the PF (Pilot Flying) asked me to cycle the FD's (Flight Directors). This was at approximately 1000 ft.; to my recollection; and I complied; ensuring the correct switches (FD's). After cycling them off then on; all appeared normal and the PF verbalized this. A few moments later; however; we were below GS which I noticed when I looked back outside and saw the PAPI. I remember hearing the aural 'Glideslope' warning once; but I do not remember exactly when this occurred. We did not receive any other alerts. The FD had been centered on my side; but I don't recall the GS indicator position. I did not notice the FMAs (Flight Mode Annunciators); which were likely no longer in approach mode: V/S (Vertical Speed) and HDG (Heading Hold) Hold; as I believe we never re-selected the Approach tile. I was looking outside at the PAPI which was red; and was starting to say this when the PF leveled off. He made airspeed corrections as well. We were red over white and stable at 500 ft. I did note then the GS indicated we were slightly low; consistent with a non-coincident PAPI. Landing was uneventful and we were VMC the entire approach with a visual clearance.The approach appeared normal to me until the PF asked me to cycle the FD's. Even immediately after; the aircraft appeared to be in the correct altitude/attitude. As I was focusing on making sure I had selected the correct switches (FD's); it took that small amount of time for the actual aircraft position to become apparent to me. I viewed my centered FD; which appeared normal; and visually crosschecked the PAPI's; which were abnormal - red over red; at approximately 800-700 ft. This led to a moment of confusion and I was not focused on the FMA's; which were likely in basic mode after cycling the FD's. As far as I remember; we never re-selected the Approach tile. With the delayed recognition of being low; receiving an aural GS alert; leveling off; throttle movement and airspeed monitoring; and thinking about a possible go around; a lot was occurring in quick succession. I failed to recognize the situation early and this could have led to an undesired state if left unchecked.My focus was outside until becoming distracted by the call to cycle FD's. My focus then shifted inside. While doing so; I failed to effectively monitor the aircraft position; PAPI; and FMA status. Focus must be on 'flying the aircraft' first and being a good pilot monitoring. I should have been more proactive in verbalizing the aircraft state; once noticed; and my attention should always be on active monitoring. I should have gathered more information about what the CA (Captain) saw when we cycled the FD's. Finally; my failure to notice the start of deviation from red over white to red over pink would have allowed more of a buffer to correct other failures; such as reselecting Approach tile or verifying the GS indicator against the PAPI as well as cross checking CA/FO indications.

column121: At XA:44; the Company asked the Dispatcher to divert an airborne flight to another location for operational necessity. The Dispatcher was able to maintain visual flight following via the software and communicate with the flight via communication software; but was unable to make further changes to the route during this time. (The crew subsequently took a direct routing.) There were numerous computer outages / updates taking place through out the day; making operational control via secondary means; difficult at best.  Supervisor had just come on duty and had not logged into the computer before relieving the previous supervisor. He then got into a backlog of issues including this one. Supervisor should log in and familiarize himself with today's operations and issues before relieving the previous supervisor. Review with the Supervisor the importance of moving a diverted flight in a timely manner so that operational control can be maintained by the dispatcher. Schedule important computer outages / updates for a day that is less busy (IE a weekend).

We would later recall the ramp agent remarking as he closed us out that he had been called out to work this flight; and that it was not his normal flight. As we received pushback clearance; we also received an ACARS message indicating 'FOM 10.37 Dry Ice Supplemental Procedures in Effect.' I was asked to acknowledge the message via ACARS; which I did (as I understand it) to modify the FPR and make the flight legal to dispatch. I held the push as the First Officer got out of his seat; pulled out the monitors; and powered them up. I verbalized that the APU was already running with the packs on; that we would perform a 2-engine taxi; and we would need to start the APU after landing at ZZZ1. I assumed (wrongly) that I had missed the FOM 10.37 reference in the DG paperwork I had signed; AND that the FO had already provided a copy to the ramp agent while closing; and had RETAINED a folded copy of in his back pocket. We continued the push; now 2 hrs; 34 min late for an uneventful departure. When we leveled off; we reviewed the DG paperwork again and pulled out the 10.37 procedures in the FOM. It was then I discovered that the paperwork did not have more than 1000 KG of dry ice; that it did not have a reference to FOM 10.37 and that the FOM procedure also prohibited lives onboard; which we had (chicks). I felt relieved for our safety that we had air on the aircraft while conducting our preflight and waiting on the load for well over 90 minutes; although we had no knowledge of the dry ice during that timeframe; and the hot weather conditions were the only thing driving us to maintain airflow on the aircraft. While I am confident that we did not willingly break any FARs; I am not confident that we received dry ice updates in a timely manner; that we were dispatched with the right paperwork; nor that we met company policy prohibiting live animals while traveling with more than 1000 KG of dry ice per FOM 10.37. Excessive delays and ground crew changes likely drove some of these issues; and we should have pulled the paperwork and recalled the 'lives prohibited' part of the exemption; however I do believe receiving a 10.37 exemption while conducting a push was excessively late in the game and was not a recipe for successful compliance for this flight. Late notification during a push.Ground personnel ensure checklists are followed to generate 10.37 Supplemental paperwork early on. Lives are considered in this equation. Crew notified in time to mitigate safety issues with airflow while preflighting. If notified this late; crew would be best served to stay at or get towed back to gate; review FOM and DG paperwork. If in error; obtain new paperwork.
column123: Because of delays caused by weather and volume; we pushed off the gate 2 hours and 40 minutes late. We had completed all of our pre-departure duties and were in the process of pushing back off the gate when we got an ACARS message from [Operations] alerting us to add to the flight release that we were dispatched with 'FOM 10.37 Dry Ice Supplemental Procedures in Effect'. The Captain acknowledged the message and said he was familiar with the procedure and we would continue as he discussed items regarding the procedure. (I've only dispatched with the exemption a few other times; however; I felt comfortable with what was required.) I further stated that we were already planning a two engine taxi and that we would need to run the APU upon arrival in ZZZ1; leave the APU running at the Gate and Notify the Ramp personnel in ZZZ. I also retrieved the Drager CO2 which the Captain turned on for us both and we wore per the procedure. The Captain made the comment that we could review the rest of the procedure while in cruise. The Taxi and Departure was routine. Once we got to cruise; the Captain and I reviewed the Supplemental Procedures and our DG paperwork. We realized that the paperwork was incorrect and showed live animals onboard in the ABK which is not allowed per the FOM. Cause: I think multiple things contributed to the event. First; the Hub has been severely delayed since the COVID Crisis Started. I think everyone is a bit 'tired' of this continued 'Peak like Operation.' I know the Ramp Agent who closed out our flight prior to push made a comment that he was unfamiliar with our flight and was working another Flight when told to close our flight out so we could push. Further; it was a long duty day for me and the Captain was eager to get to the layover. It was our first leg together; and while the Captain seemed very capable; we weren't used to flying together yet. I also believe the long and unfortunate cultural norm of 'rushing' started to creep in given that we were so late. I also had the thought that wondered if [Operations] had sent an ACARS message to the wrong flight regarding the Supplemental Procedures given that it was coming so late. Suggestions: My biggest frustration is that normally I am very good at slowing down a situation that is rushed and take pride in my attention to detail assuring that things are accounted for and speak up when I think we need to take more time. Unfortunately; given the late nature of the [Operations] message regarding the Supplemental Procedures coming during the pushback; and assuming the Captain was more familiar with the procedure; I did not suggest to the Captain that we return to the gate and or sit off the gate once pushed back to review the procedure and paperwork to assure we complied with all company procedures. At the time I felt comfortable enough with the Captains brief of the procedure and reviewing the procedure while en-route given that we verbally talked about the procedures required. That was a mistake and something I normally don't do. I never assume in the airplane and always prefer to verify/review information on my own. I will be more diligent on not allowing such complacency. I should have insisted that we stop and assure we were in full compliance considering that I hadn't had the Supplemental Dry Ice Procedure often. Further; what is disturbing; is that the Ramp Agent that closed out our flight obviously was not aware of what was onboard the airplane. He was unaware; and it had not been commented to him that we had the excessive amount of Dry Ice and Live Animals on board. Further; a checklist needs to be better developed for the Ramp to use; especially with notifying [Operations] and the Flight Crew in a timely manner of the dry ice supplemental procedure need. We had been on the airplane with doors closed and engines off/packs off in various stages of configuration with no idea that we were carrying the excessive amount of Dry Ice. Also; within that checklist; the ramp should be require to verify that the flight crew is notified of the Procedure prior pushback. During Pushback is not the time to tell the crew of a cumbersome operational procedure. Further [Operations should have advised a return to the gate to assure that paperwork and procedures were applied correctly; safely/legally considering they knew we had pushed back off the gate and needed to address this procedure. Lastly; I think in general from a Flight Ops perspective; two things. More training on the Dry Ice Supplemental Procedures should be stressed during Recurrent training. I am aware of the Procedures in the FOM; FM and QRH; but really it is a procedure that isn't discussed much given its importance. Further; I need to do better as a First Officer to question the Captain in the need to properly review the procedures to assure compliance as soon as something comes up like this comes up. Again; I'm very frustrated with my performance and certainly will be more diligent.

column121: I was holding short of the runway and was aware there was traffic incoming (Last radio call was 20 miles I believe). I called and asked for position of the inbound single engine aircraft two times; and no radio call was announced. I also checked my garmin unit for ADSB data and there was none. I made the decision to announce a back taxi radio call on Runway XX and proceed onto the runway to back taxi. At about 1;000 feet left; I noticed a plane executing a go around on the runway; and flew over me at approx an altitude of 200 feet above. I then called if he was on frequency and he responded 'yeah'. I asked if he made any radio calls and he said 'no I missed the last radio call'; and asked if he heard my back-taxi call to which he responded yes. I proceeded to turn around at the departure end of the runway and depart without incident.  In summary I made 3 radio calls that were unanswered; did a visual search before entering the runway before back taxi; and checked for ADSB to see if the plane was in the airport environment before my decision to back taxi.

column121: After landing at PANC; directed to taxi via Taxiway R and TWY U. The weather was very dark with light rain and wet taxiways. As the aircraft approached TWY U; the Captain was focused on finding centerline of TWY U from TWY R. As the aircraft committed to the turn; the First Officer noticed a white Ford van enter TWY U crossing north to south on the access road parallel to TWY R. The First Officer alerted the Captain to the intrusion. He slammed on the brakes and was able to stop the aircraft. As the aircraft was stopping; the First Officer reached up to turn on all landing lights in an attempt to alert the van. After the van cleared to the south; the First Officer alerted Tower to the incident. As we were parking the aircraft; we were able to hear ANC Tower directing security to stop the subject van. This event was caused by an inattentive or negligent driver that failed to yield to an aircraft taxiing on dark; wet night. The drivers around the airport (this driver in particular) need to be reminded about the limited maneuverability of aircraft on the taxiways and the need to be conscientious about yielding to aircraft on taxiways. This is particularly important when heavy aircraft are attempting to taxi on dark; wet (slick) taxiways.

column121: The purpose of this [report] is to draw attention to/document possible maintenance malpractice during ground operations for flight X; DATE; ZZZ to ZZZ1 on aircraft X. At approximately 20 minutes prior to block out we were informed by maintenance of fuel venting from our left wing in the vicinity of the '#1 surge tank' and that they would need to transfer some fuel to fix the issue. The maintenance representative (rep) began to transfer fuel from the #1 main tank (13.1 indicated qty; max 13.3) to the center wing tank (cw; ind 0.2) to try and reduce the pressure from the '#1 reserve' tank (actually #2 res; ind 3.9; max 4.0). After watching this unfold for a moment and overhearing the rep discussing the issue with someone on the phone; I asked why they were transferring from #1 main to the cw tank? The answer I received was somewhat surprising and disappointing... 'to reduce pressure from the fuel draining out of the #1 reserve'. I informed them that there was not a #1 reserve... The rep on the phone had no idea the aircraft was a 747-400 and said he thought it was a 747-8 which prompted some confusion for the local rep. I informed the rep that this aircraft is a 747-400 and there was no #1 reserve that it's a #2 reserve which drains into the #2 main tank; not the #1 main. Both the local rep/mechanic and the rep on the phone were surprised by this... after some discussion the next step they pondered caused additional concern... their next idea was to transfer fuel from the #2/3 tanks to the #1/4 main tanks. I asked them to stop immediately and asked why we would do that? They seemed puzzled by the question. The answer we eventually got was that they planned to transfer 'two thousand' with the goal of relieving pressure in the #2 reserve so it would stop venting. I asked if he knew that the outboards couldn't hold that much. He had no idea what the capacity of the outboard tanks was; no idea that we couldn't just drain from the reserves (earlier discussion); didn't know the #2/3 mains were well below capacity (Ind 22.3; max 38.1) already and in general; did not seem to understand how the fuel system on a 747-400 worked. In the meantime the fuel venting (caused apparently by a slight over servicing of a fuel tank combined with expansion due to warm temperatures) slowed and eventually stopped; as they also apparently had decided (after leaving the flight deck) to use the refueling panel on the wing to move fuel from the #2/3 main tanks to the cw tank (final cw qty = 8.9). Upon completion of this exercise the venting stopped; the fuel spill was cleaned up; I (the PIC) asked for a new wt/bal from the load master (cw indicating 8.9 vs 0.2 originally); we received the amended wt/bal; ran new performance and eventually blocked out 49 minutes late. After starting to push back I commanded the push be stopped as we determined there was a door open somewhere since the block out time was not indicated on the ACARS. I double checked the EICAS confirming there were no door messages. We then informed tow crew it might be a panel near the strut (per msg pulled from center CDU). They reset/reclosed the door and we subsequently departed for ZZZ1. The entire episode is very concerning as the mx reps seemed to be guessing at how the fuel system worked versus knowing how it worked. This could have resulted in a larger spill as well as a myriad of other issues. As a side note; after all was completed the local mechanic/Mx rep was very apologetic; was trying hard to rectify/stop the leak and honestly very respectful throughout the process as he tried hard; but struggled to do the right thing due to being given incorrect inputs via telephone from another mx rep.I'm not a mechanic but it is unacceptable to have maintenance personnel working on the airplane who do not understand the systems. They must be appropriately trained or under supervision. This situation was unacceptable and does not inspire confidence in the capability/credibilityof the ZZZ maintenance personnel.

column121: The flight was progressing normally until we updated weather prior to coast out. We were unable to maintain radio contact with Stockholm Radio to get a phone patch with the FOO. But we knew that the weather at our ETOPS alternate had deteriorated and was unusable as an alternate. The flight path was discontinued and we went into holding at the direction of Shanwick Radio before the RESNO intersection. After a while; we were able to establish contact with Iceland Radio and we got a clear phone patch to the FOO. After some discussion; it was determined that the flight could not continue and we were to turn back to ZZZZ. Clearance was obtained from Shanwick and we were heading towards ZZZZ. We needed to burn a lot of fuel in order to land under the maximum landing weight. So a lower altitude was obtained to aid in burning fuel. The First Officer needed to use the bathroom. Before the IRO could take the FO (First Officer) seat; the max airspeed warning sounded. I was very busy working with ATC to complete our route and program the FMC. During the programming sequence; the only speed in the FMC was the cruise altitude of M.80. The autopilot was engaged with LNAV and VNAV selected and the speed window closed. The FMA was indicating VNAV Speed and the speed bug and airspeed indication were both over the VMO (Maximum Operating Speed) by 3-5 knots. There was nothing in the descent page as the route and crossing altitudes were still being programmed. The VMO was exceeded by 3-5 knots at 20;000 ft. MSL. After a quick recovery from the overspeed; the remaining programing of the FMS was completed and the remainder of the flight progressed normally. The flight was completed and the overspeed was noted in the logbook.

column121: Illegal departure due equipment.Flew VOR based departure procedure without RNAV (Arear Navigation) or GPS (Global Positioning System); as required by NOTAM (Notice To Airman)Arrived to the plane (Aircraft X) in preparation for flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1 and discovered both FMCs (Flight Management Computers)were deferred.  The Captain and I discussed the conduct of the flight without the use of either FMC.  I reviewed the route of flight based on short range navigation.  The release showed that we were filed for the SID departure; which required we depart Runway X; straight out until reaching 19 DME from ZZZ VOR; then turn to a heading and intercept an inbound course to VOR.DME information was not present on the ground; I assumed it would be present in the [air] because of terrain features in the area. I noticed there was no DME information after takeoff.  The Captain suggested using FMC navigation data for the turn.  Following the turn; I switched back to heading select in combination with short range NAV (Navigation).Upon closer inspection and cross check; the following details were discovered;1) SID; which is a VOR based departure; had a NOTAM; 'SID DEPARTURE...TAKEOFF RWY X NA EXCEPT FOR AIRCRAFT EQUIPPED WITH SUITABLE RNAV SYSTEM WITH GPS; ZZZ TACAN OUT OF SERVICE'2) Right DME not receiving DME from any sourceA clearance via the SID departure made sense to me; as it was a VOR based departure.  I believed all components of the departure were functioning since that is how we were cleared.  I also believed that short range NAV would be sufficient to fly the departure legally since that is the equipment the departure was predicated on; and the absence of any notes requiring RNAV equipment on the departure procedure.The oversight is easy to understand when considering that clearance via a departure procedure based on short range NAV was expected due to lack of RNAV capability.  Clearance via the SID would not raise any red flags regarding the lack of GPS equipment required as the departure is not based on RNAV equipment.  The failure is not a single source failure; as these details were missed by dispatch; flight crew; and ATC; as they cleared us via a departure requiring RNAV when; to the best of my knowledge; the RNAV related equipment codes were removed.Spend a little more time reviewing details; such as NOTAMs; especially during abnormal procedures.Given the lack of GPS equipped aircraft; file departure procedures not requiring GPS; as a matter of general practice.
column123: Upon arrival at the aircraft (Aircraft X) to fly the first leg of flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1; we discovered the IRS (Inertial Reference System) NAV (Navigation Only) ONLY discrepancy we had noted in the logbook two days prior had not yet been corrected. In fact; because of this; both FMC's (Flight Management Computers) were now deferred. I called the dispatcher and ensured he changed the strip to reflect that we were no longer RNAV (Area Navigation) capable. The FO (First Officer) and I discussed what was available from the FMC's and we determined: even though they were working and we knew it was only the IRS updating function which was not functioning properly; because the entire FMC was deferred none of the functions were legally available. We discussed short range NAV procedures for a flat panel aircraft and reviewed the filed SID and the route beyond to ZZZ1. Because of this deferral and the discussion it caused; I was only able to quickly review the NOTAMS (Notice to Airman) In the time remaining prior to departure. After takeoff; we quickly determined we were not receiving ZZZ VORTAC's DME (Distance Measuring Equipment). Knowing the position in the IRS's was still good; I encouraged the FO (First Officer) to follow the FMC generated magenta course until I could dial in another NAVAID in which was suitable for navigation. I quickly determined the problem was two fold: ZZZ DME was out and the right VOR was not receiving DME at all (from any source). Once out of the critical phase of flight and high volume area; I again checked the NOTAMS to see if ZZZ DME was out of service. I found the following NOTAM (partly hidden by a staple): SID...TAKEOFF RWY Y; X NA EXCEPT FOR AIRCRAFT EQUIPPED WITH SUITABLE RNAV SYSTEM WITH GPS; ZZZ TACAN OUT OF SERVICE (see photo). Not only were we not legal to file or fly this departure because of the dual FMS deferral but this aircraft was NEVER legal for this departure as it has yet to updated with the addition of GPS. No deviations occurred but we should NEVER have filed; been cleared or flown this SID. This entire situation would have been avoided if Company had done any one of three things in advance of this event: 1) Upgrade its fleet to modern navigation standards by installing GPS. 2) Repair the minor discrepancy rather than defer both FMC systems in their entirety.3) Flight Control reviewing the NOTAMS and not filing us for a departure we were not legal to fly.Having said that; I allowed time constraints and training an FO just off IOE (Initial Operating Experience) on highly non-standard procedures to distract me from a through review of the NOTAMS. I also believe the NOTAM itself was poorly worded; in that it used the term TACAN rather than DME. Civilian pilots and dispatchers do not generally use this military term (civilian aircraft are not TACAN equipped).

column121: Landed in ZZZ. FO (First Officer) started APU for tow-in; it shut down. I started it; being careful not to let the start switch spring back to Run. It ran fine but we advised Maintenance of a possible problem. Went to the hotel for the four-hour layover. Returning to the aircraft; Maintenance said the APU had shut down on them and they deferred it. This aircraft had APU problems in the past. The plan was to tow the aircraft under battery power only and have the huffer and ground power waiting on Taxiway XX. Starting an engine in the blocks was not an option because of construction on Taxiway XY. We did the Before Start Checklist before ground power was disconnected. I did not request the Engine Start Checklist because there was no point in turning on the fuel and hydraulic pumps if we were on battery power only. We were pushed back and then we were asked to set brakes so the tug could reposition to pull the aircraft instead of push it. Setting the brakes at this point may have depleted the hydraulic pressure in the brake system. The brake pressure gauge was unpowered and reading zero. We were towed from Taxiway XY to Taxiway XX. I closed my window as I could see the huffer on my side of the aircraft and knew it would get noisy during the start. The FO still had his window open for ventilation. Once stopped at the designated spot; I was asked to set the parking brake. External power had not been connected yet and the brake pressure gauge was still unpowered. I set the brake and responded 'brakes set.' I did not give permission to disconnect the tow bar. External power came on and the cockpit flood lights came on. The taxiway is not illuminated and the cockpits lights reflecting off my closed window made it difficult for me to see outside. The FO's window was open and he noticed a separation developing between the aircraft and the ground power cart on his side and also the tug. He called out that we were rolling about the same time Ground called out a warning. He stomped on the brakes and I followed but there was no effect. He called out to put on the hydraulic pumps as I was reaching for them. The ground power cord stayed connected for just a few seconds but it was enough to power the hydraulic pumps and get the aircraft stopped. Taxiway XX is steeply sloped for a taxiway and it didn't take long for the aircraft to get moving. If external power had not come on for those few seconds; we would have rolled a long way backward with no nosewheel steering; no brakes; and quickly moving.The ground power cord had pulled free from the aircraft as well as the pneumatic connections. I kept a steady pressure on the brake pedals while Ground sorted things out. I don't know if they had any chocks available. The FO volunteered to take over the brakes for me. I said I could set the parking brake but after discussion decided not to and I released the parking brake without ever having taken pressure off the pedals. Maintenance said [another Company] had to tow this aircraft a couple of days ago with the same situation. I asked why this didn't happen to that aircraft. They said the tow bar had not been disconnected before ground power was plugged in. The chain of events leading up to this started with a deferred APU; not being able to start an engine in the blocks; having to set the parking brake so the tug could turn around; parking on a steep slope; and disconnecting the tow bar too soon and without permission. Looking back; I wish I had foreseen this possibility and told Ground not to disconnect the tow bar yet and had not said; 'Parking brake set.'

column121: Crew called to advised DG (Dangerous Goods) paperwork for can in position 6 was not placed in the can. DG specialist told them it could be placed in the ADG (Accessible Dangerous Goods) can in position 1 instead. I spoke with the freight recovery specialist; who spoke with the ramp agent and DG specialist and advised it was acceptable to put it in the ADG can. Still concerned; the crew spoke with the Duty Officer; who called Flight Safety. Flight safety advised it was fine to proceed with the paperwork in the ADG can. Captain sent an email today advising 'This morning I received an email from the Flight Safety Manager; and he said placing that Form in the ADG can was actually not correct; and that we moved the freight with an improperly labeled can as a result.'DG specialist and Flight Safety should have been better trained and/or unafraid to correct an error causing a delay.
column123: Ramp Agent presented us with the DG paperwork and proceeded in telling us that an additional form that he had was supposed to be in the IDG (Inaccessible Dangerous Goods) ULD (Unit Load Devise) in position 6. I informed him that it had to be placed in the assigned ULD and told him to let his manager know. After he left; I looked the policy in the DG manual to confirm my thoughts. I called [Operations] and told them what was going on; and they did not have a problem with the outbound making it right because we were on a weather delay. After a while the Ramp Agent returned with his manger. Manager proceeded to tell us [Operations] told them it would be ok to place the label in the ADG ULD. We called [Operations] back and had him to confirm this with the Fright Recover specialist. They both said it would be ok. Before we blocked out; we called the DO and asked him about this subject again. He made a couple of phone calls including Flight Safety and they all said we were good to go. Outbound load employee not following DG procedures. The outbound load personnel was notified of the correct procedures and was given ample time to make the correction.

column121: While reaching down for the rudder trim knob during cruise; I inadvertently deployed the flaps to 20%. The aircraft ballooned 200-300 ft. quickly as I corrected and notified ATC of the situation. The flaps never reached an over speed condition. I looked to my checklists for a solution to the problem. I then checked the circuit breaker panel. I advised ATC that I would need a block altitude to slow down within flap operating range; extend the flaps to 100%; and then retract them. This has worked on the ground in the past when flaps fail to retract after landing; always written up in the AML (Aircraft Maintenance Logbook). The flaps failed to retract upon the initial attempt so I proceeded to try cycling the flap handle again. When [I] retracted the flaps from the fully extended position on the second effort; I was unable to remain within the requested block of altitude. With the resultant loss of lift while also visually determining if the flaps had retracted on both the flap position indicator and outside the aircraft; I exercised PIC (Pilot in Command) authority to quickly [request priority handling]. Once the aircraft was stabilized and I was able to confidently determine which configuration the aircraft flaps were in; I notified ATC that I [no longer needed priority handling] and would then proceed on course. [I was] instantly aware of the change in flap position via [the] 200-300 ft. gain in altitude and forward pressure required to combat this. Human error caused the inadvertent deployment of flaps. Flight control malfunction caused the inability to retract the flaps. [I] notified ATC immediately when [the] flaps were inadvertently deployed and also when I was unable to retract the flaps - flight control malfunction. I ran my abnormal and emergency checklists; but neither addressed the current situation. I wasted no time in [requesting priority handling] when I was unable to maintain the block altitude given. My first priority was to fly the plane; but also make the world bigger and get more people involved. Once I was confident in the safe operation of the aircraft and its ability to complete our mission; I again advised ATC of my intentions. Being more conscious with hand movements in the flight deck will prevent this event from occurring again. If I would have first confirmed with my eyes before reaching for the rudder trim knob; I believe I would not have inadvertently bumped the flap handle and deployed the flaps to 20%. I also believe that a QRH for the [aircraft] would have assisted me in determining whether the smartest course of action would be to leave the flaps in the 20% extended configuration or cycle the flap handle. The greatest risk in cycling the flaps to 100% and then 0% is that there is no guarantee they will retract once fully extended. Hindsight being 20:20 I believe leaving the flaps in the 20% configuration for the remainder of the flight would have been the better choice. I have learned from the situation and will teach others from this experience.

column121: After being vectored over the airport and sequenced behind multiple heavy jets; I was cleared for the visual approach to 35R at SDF. The last vector to final was a shallow intercept angle and I mistakenly identified a warehouse as being part of the [company] ramp. This led to partial spatial disorientation which allowed me to believe I was 1.5 miles from the airport instead of the actual 2.5 miles. The tower controller gave me an altitude alert and the altimeter setting; which prompted me to add power and reevaluate my location to the airport. I then reset my glide path and had a stabilized approach to landing with no further issues. I believe a contributing factor was the lengthy duty day that also included a stop at SDF about 10 hours earlier. Additionally;  I was vectored over the airport and looked down at the airport environment to identify the [company] ramps and the FBO ramp where I would be offloading/loading freight; which added to my belief that I had correctly identified part of the airport environment. To prevent this from happening; I could have switched my CDI to follow the ILS (which I had loaded). Also; since I was cleared for the visual I could have turned more to intercept final further out instead of following a shallow intercept angle.

column121: Began initial descent into ZZZZ. The controller called to change the STAR. I had to ask 3 times to repeat the prescribed STAR to be flown. His English was very broken. Traffic on the frequency was light. We determined a change of STARs. I input into the FMS and confirmed and executed with the Captain. By this time we were either over [the IAF] to or just past the point. The aircraft overflew [the fix]. The Captain went into heading select and turned to course. Two to three miles past [the fix]; the aircraft was back on an intercept outbound [from the fix]. Then the controller said turn to a heading to intercept inbound course; which we had already initiated. Continuing descent the controller instructed us to fly the circuit which was part of the STAR and we did as planned. During the descent the controller gave us 5 altitude step downs to comply with; 4 of the 5 were then subsequently modified back to a higher altitude. After the compliance with circuit instructions; controller changed the runway. I then reprogrammed the FMS; and confirmed execute with the Captain. After so many changes by the controller and workload was lowered in the cockpit; I queried the controller one final time to ensure we were all on same page. I stated to controller confirm ILS XXR; controller said negative ILS XXL; are you ready to commence approach. I quickly for 3rd time reprogrammed the FMS for ILS XXL confirmed with the Captain and executed. I then told controller ready to commence; and then briefed the Captain on differences of approaches; and new Baro; and landing distances. We landed uneventfully.Poor English by controller almost inaudible. Very late approach instructions modifications. Could be solved if controller gave us changes to STAR and approach a few minutes prior to descent instead of at last moment; and past Anchor points on STAR.
column123: We were filed to [the IAF] and we set up for the ILS Approach. As we approached [the fix] the controller issued a new arrival but we had difficulty understanding the new clearance [due to] language problems. Finally it was determined after 3 difficult queries what we were to fly. After installing the new clearance into the FMS the Aircraft did not make the turn towards [the] next point. As pilot flying I recognized the overshoot and made a correction back to course just prior to ATC issuing vectors. During the arrival numerous runway changes were issued and at least 5 or more altitude instructions given. Just prior to base turn the First Officer queried the controller one final time to confirm ILS XXR. The controller said negative ILS XXL. We quickly for 3rd time reprogrammed the FMS for the ILS XXL; briefed and executed an uneventful landing on XXL.Language problems which caused confusion and delayed FMS programming on our part. Late arrival insertion caused overshoot. Overshoot caused workload to increase. Do a better job anticipating what other options may be available to your crew and get an early confirmation on what arrival to expect. Better to reprogram the FMS after sequencing to the next point then forcing a FMS change close to a turn point.

column121: Afternoon launch - sort late 90 minutes.  My freight recovery specialist; informed me Aircraft X blocked even though the ramp notified the crew to wait for new DG (dangerous goods) paperwork.  ACARS was sent to the crew to hold; new DG paperwork on the way.  I asked the Captain to call me on the phone to explain that the current DG paper work indicated no DG however; there was IDG (international dangerous goods) onboard and new paperwork is required.  We both agreed a block turn back was the best way to handle this situation.  Aircraft returned to the blocks for correction of DG paperwork; new release was sent and weight and balance (per Captain's request). Ramp agent made a mistake most likely due to high workload/task saturation and work distractions/interruptions.  The sort was over 2 hours late and the load teams were overwhelmed.  I had at least 4 adhocs with double legs (out and back) and some with 3 legs. This flight was on hold during most of the sort along with other flights; then decisions were made to reroute the adhocs and add legs.  There was a lot of confusion and decisions were being made last minute. We are in unprecedented times.  Everyone is doing their best.  Some of us are better equipped to handle the constant changes and challenges.  Errors will be made; I am glad we were able to correct it and move on.

column121: This flight was planned on a route that went through ZZZZ.  In my pre-flight planning process; I checked the enroute NOTAMs by loading all the enroute FIR boundaries and then using 'control-F' and searching the enroute NOTAMs for applicable airways.  Today; there were no such hits when performing this NOTAM checking method.  Unfortunately; there was a NOTAM for ZZZZ that had been issued just before I arrived for work:...DUE TO COVID-19...ATS WILL NOT BE AVAILABLE. ATS CONTINGENCY PLAN(AIC A11/18) FOR ZZZZ1 FIR ACT.                                                                                     The flight had been airborne for some time; but was still in ZZZZ2 airspace when the crew advised me that they were being re-routed out of ZZZZ airspace - the re-route was minimal and after considerable effort (due to non-existent or out-of-date info in AIR for ZZZZ and ZZZZ3) I was finally able to speak with ZZZZ3 ATC and obtain an expected route through their airspace; and then I was able to advise the crew of the routing.  The amount of en-route FIR boundary NOTAMs is daunting - impossible to read these for every international flight --- therefore using the 'Control-F' to search for applicable airways allows the Dispatcher to quickly determine if there are any en-route implications to the flight.  Of course; if there are no associated airways with a NOTAM as in the case of the situation affecting this flight; then pertinent closures can be missed.  In addition; since the crews do not receive a copy of the FIR boundary NOTAMs; this scenario leaves the Dispatcher as the single point of failure.Be smarter when it comes to FIR boundary NOTAMs.  Utilize a resource like 'SmartNotam' to weed through all the FIR boundary NOTAMs and then provide both the crew and the dispatcher a condensed list of applicable FIR boundary NOTAMs to read and decipher.

column121: Operating flight as Pilot Monitoring. We were deviating to avoid weather along the route. We were cleared direct to ZZZZZ waypoint and asked for a deviation around weather but was initially denied. We were only authorized a deviation right of course in which were able to avoid the first TCU (Towering Cumulus) but the wind direction and velocity forced us into the second TCU as we were turning back onto course. Prior to entering the TCU the wings were leveled and we experienced a climb of approximately 700-800 ft. During the altitude excursion ATC asked why we had deviated and I replied that we were currently in the TCU. The autopilot remained engaged and within approximately 10 seconds the aircraft recovering back to the assigned altitude. ATC asked again for the reason and I replied that we had entered the TCU momentarily and was back on course and assigned altitude. ATC inability to provide deviations in either direction due to weather. Better communication between ATC facilities and increased tolerances left or right of course for hazardous weather conditions.

column121: After takeoff; the Captain - pilot flying - engaged the autopilot at 500 ft. and the aircraft immediately started to level off [and] then tried to descend. He disconnected the autopilot and returned the flight path to a climb. During that time we got a GPWS 'Don't sink' aural warning. Upon later investigation we figured out what had happened. The first point on the SID; GG511. has a speed restriction of 230 kt. which was loaded in the FMS. It was his intention to load 230/005A to command 230 kt./500ft. or above at GG511 but it was inadvertently loaded as 230/005 so the FMS wanted 230 kt. at 500 ft. at GG511; when the autopilot was engaged it tried to capture 500 ft. The rest of the departure and flight were uneventful. [The cause was] a mistake loading the FMS. [I suggest to] properly load the FMS and better cross-check from the pilot monitoring - myself.

column121: The aircraft's left fuel indicator was MEL'd and was blank. Following the MEL procedure; the Captain spoke with the Maintenance crew about the fuel numbers. Before our arrival; Maintenance accomplished the fuel stick procedure to verify the amount of fuel in each wing and total fuel to upload. We where told each side was balanced and the total fuel load was 37;500 lbs. Maintenance provided us with the chart they used to load the fuel and their explanation in writing. Everything they showed us looked correct. However; in flight we began to wonder about the accuracy as the Captain examined the papers he gave us and the current readout on the remaining right indicator. The fuel flow was matched and consistent between both engines the entire flight. The calculated number in the FMC was off from the right side indicator. There is no other way to tell if we had an imbalance to my knowledge; that's why the starting fuel load is critical to have balanced. As we approached ZZZ the Captain disconnected the A/P to feel for an imbalance. The aircraft was trimmed perfectly and neither side felt heavy. The Captain landed the aircraft normally. On the post flight checks Maintenance was outside sticking the tanks. The Captain asked him what the numbers were and he said 11;000 lbs of fuel remained in the left tank; 6;000 lbs in the right and 600 pounds in the center. The Captain couldn't believe there seemed to be an imbalance of 5;000 lbs. I'm not sure that was true because the aircraft seemed to fly wings level in flight. When we left I never got the chance to see if Maintenance had incorrectly calculated those numbers of if there actually was an imbalance.

column121: I neglected to notice that the Airworthiness Certificate was missing from the plane in the morning. It should be in a little pocket on the front of the pilot's door side pocket that's difficult to get the certificates out of it. And without pulling all the certificates out of the pocket; it's not possible to make sure that the 3 certificates are in there (registration; airworthiness; and radio license). Only the front one can be seen. And if we are constantly pulling all the certificates out that's a lot of extra wear and tear on the certificates. I happened to pull the certificates out of the pocket while waiting for the evening freight and discovered that the Airworthiness Certificate was missing. Dispatch figured out how to make it legal for me to get home. Perhaps have 3 pockets (or one wide pocket) on the door instead of just one small pocket so all 3 certificates can be seen without pulling them out of the pocket. That way they're easy to check without any wear and tear. Or make the pocket larger so that they are easier to pull out.

It was not my intention to operate the aircraft without the required documents on board.

column121: Initially planned 09R Dep as per Flight Plan and current ATIS. Briefed RANUX4G Dep. After obtaining clearance and new ATIS; Departure Runway was changed to 27L. Runway change procedures followed and new briefing for the RANUX4A from 27L briefed; FMS perf verified; data changed etc. While taxiing out we were told to contact GND at spot (removed). We did so and were given instructions to taxi; Spot; Q RWY27L. A discussion ensued with all 3 pilots about whether or not this allowed us to choose our own route to 27L. During this time I slowed to a taxi speed of about 4-5 knots; barely rolling; to give everyone a chance to absorb the call and catch up. We decided to err on the side of clarity and asked if we could taxi Spot; B; Q4; 27L. The answer back was no. What I heard was: Taxi Spot; BD8; D; Q; 27L. Ok; upscale the iPad and look for the route. Everyone else was doing the same. I was having a problem finding BD8; verbalized it and the RFO said I'll give you 'progressive'. We were still going less than 10 KTS when I made the turn to follow M in front of the Fire Station. Because of the lighting; signage; and the fact that I undershot the turn to stay on M; we rolled barely onto MD2. As soon as I realized my error; I stopped (cursed) and set the brake. I told the crew what happened and that we could not make the turn back to M and we would be unable to make a right turn onto any other taxiway to continue east bound. At that time; Ground called and told us that it appeared we undershot our turn and were on MD2. We agreed and asked what she wanted us to do. We were given a standby. During that time we discussed the only way out was to continue on MD2; MD1D; BD6; B and get going the other way. Ground came back on and asked if we could do exactly that. We concurred and we were given that exact clearance plus from B; BD9; Q; Q4 to 27L. It is nitpicking but I don't believe QD1 was ever given between D and Q. In any event. We got turned around. Didn't turn in a prohibited direction; didn't drag a gear truck through the mud or non-stressed area; didn't have to get towed and didn't shut down any taxiways or inhibit any other aircraft from their taxi. We got everyone on the same page and taxied to the end and took off. Once in the air; we debriefed the event as a crew. The initial taxi instructions were vague. The subsequent taxi instructions became confusing. The FO apparently didn't understand the taxi instruction; confusing BD8 for B; D8. I couldn't find BD8 on my chart while scaling up and sliding the chart around to understand the route. The RFO thought he had the route clarified only to lose the bubble at the end and was unable to communicate clearly what he was seeing. The signage in that area is abysmal. The lighting is glaring and the markings on the taxiways are not very clear/faint. And in our case; by the time we could verify our position; it was too late to fix it.With ongoing construction and changes at CDG; with being there previously and given taxi down B to QB7; Q4; 27L; etc. Even though we reviewed the taxi options and the standard taxi pages; we were given something unexpected and were unable to resolve what should have been a simple problem. I didn't realize how much of a problem it was until I undershot M on M2. I thought we had it resolved. I should have stopped; set the brake and sorted it out. Something that would also help would be to have ATC give instruction similar to ' Taxi from spot M via North Route 22; hold point XXX; RW27L'. We try to not set expectation bias by briefing TAXI routes. When they are given piecemeal instead of as a package; it gets confusing sometimes. We were finally able to alleviate these issues in CAN with canned routes. Not finger pointing; just a suggestion. It was my fault.
column123: I was second RFO seated in the back in supernumerary seating; by the galley. I did notice some conversation after stopping then a left turn and some extra taxi movement and instructions. I was not seated in the cockpit during taxi out. Later I was told by the crew there was some confusion as to the finding the correct taxiway in which they were cleared. I know from experience that Paris taxi markings and lighting is subpar. There have been other occurrences in this same location. I even remember a hot topic published outlining the difficulties in taxiing in this area. Other flights have turned right onto delta and have left the prepared [surface]. I give accolades to this Captain for not falling in this trap after he had missed the correct turn on the correct taxiway. His actions saved the jet from leaving the prepared surface and allowed the flight to continue to destination and delivery of the freight; albeit with a few extra taxi clearances needed. Paris should take responsibility for these occurrences and get their taxiways up to par standards. The rest of the flight was uneventful. I believe [the cause] was confusion with taxi instructions and unable to discern the proper taxiway. My understanding is they did the right thing they were confused; they stopped the jet and figured out the problem. Then proceeded with an adequate solution.

column123: After the load was complete and the door was closed the ramp agent got our attention from the ground and said Maintenance was fixing the paperwork. I asked the pilots of both aircraft to contact the Tower and notified them that I would file a report on the event. I did not say the words 'possible pilot deviation' to Aircraft X; as required to issue a proper brasher warning. I also did not get the pilots' names; phone numbers; and certificate numbers; as I did not know that these items were required until I began filling out the report. I did note on the report that the aircraft were both air carriers; and the information was able to be obtained by referencing the callsigns.I believe the weather was a contributing factor to Aircraft X making an incorrect turn; as it was raining moderately with periodic gusting wind. A ground based radar system or a taller Control Tower would have been incredibly helpful in this circumstance; as the taxiway and runway are pretty much indistinguishable from each other at night. column121: I arrived at the aircraft as relief pilot an hour before takeoff for a cargo flight to ZZZZ. The FO was at the aircraft and had completed much of the cockpit preflight. Because it was a cargo flight I went through the cabin and secured the overhead bins and many of the storage /catering carts. The Captain arrived and we went through the standard cockpit flight preparation prior to departure. After we pushed from the gate and initiated the engine start; I realized I had not done the Pre-Fight Walk Around Inspection. I asked the FO if he had completed it and he said he had not. He thought I was doing that when I was actually securing the cabin for departure. I told the Captain I forgot to do the walk around. The Captain got clearance and we turned around on the ramp and went back into the gate. The Agent came back; hooked up the jet bridge and I went out and completed the walk around inspection. We re-accomplished all the pre-departure checks and ended up departing to ZZZZ about XX minutes late. Most of the delay was a result of getting personnel back to park us and recalling another push crew.I think that because it was a cargo flight; I was possibly distracted by some non-standard items in the cabin and got out of my habit pattern. Like most of us; I haven't been flying too much but the bottom line is that I simply forgot to do the walk around preflight and realized it after the push.In the future I will report to the FO that the walk around has been completed and as the FO I will verify with the relief pilot that it has been complete. I have been flying airplanes for XX years and have never forgotten to do a walk around inspection.

column121: We were assigned the ZZZZZX RNAV departure off Runway X at ZZZ.  The clearance was to climb via the SID; top altitude of FL230 was set in the MCP. All the fixes and altitude restrictions were correct in the FMC; I was the PM; the airplane was light; so we had a good climb rate. The PF was hand flying as we approached the first fix which has a crossing restriction of at or below 10;000. LNAV/VNAV and VNAV PTH was selected. Close to the first fix the PF called for the autopilot as the airplane started its turn to cross the fix that placed the sun directly into our face which affected our visibility. As I turned my head to get my sunshade; ATC asked if we were going to stop at 10;000 feet; we got as high as 10;300 the PF turned the autopilot off and went down to 10;000.  In this situation I think turning the autopilot on earlier would have helped. Also anticipating the sun and take steps earlier to mitigate the effects of the sun would have helped us to maintain better situational awareness.
column123: Our departure SID was the ZZZZZX.  Our departure plan was for Runway YYR per the ATIS.  During taxiout our runway assignment was changed to Runway X with the same SID.  My First Officer ran the runway change checklist and briefed me on the changes to the SID departing Runway X.  During the climbout I called for the autopilot sometime prior to 10;000 feet.  There is a fix named ZZZZZ that has a crossing altitude of 10;000 or below.  Our automation level was LNAV/VNAV with the autopilot engaged.  Approaching 10;000 feet I noticed that the FMA went to VNAV PTH.  About that time; I also got a face full of morning sunrise.  It briefly made it hard to see and I had not deployed my sunshade or put on my sunglasses yet.  When my vision adjusted to the glare of the sun I noticed that the aircraft did not level at 10;000 feet.  It overshot the altitude by 300 feet.  I disengaged the autopilot and returned to 10;000 feet.  The Controller did query us on our altitude during the overshoot.  One other piece of useful information is that the aircraft was very light.  I'm wondering if the system was respecting a G-Load vs. an altitude because I have no other explanation as to why it did not level at 10;000 feet.  Factors that I feel contributed to this event were the runway change on the ground; high airport elevation; sunrise; fatigue and maybe our light weight.  Next time I will not accept the immediate line up and wait from ATC.  Instead I would re-brief the SID so that my situational awareness would be better.

column121: Aircraft X apparently hit a set of stairs on pushback with their right wing tip unbeknownst to the crew or Marshaller. A ground crew member saw it and called it in to his supervisor; who called it in to the Ops (Airport Operations). The plane at this point was on takeoff roll and wasn't in contact with Ops via radio anymore. After getting airborne; Ops took it into their own hands and called Tower and told them to have the flight return to field. I received an message from the crew asking why the return to field; which is when I started to make calls. This happened while the crew was at 3;000 feet and turning around. Crew landed uneventfully and the plane was taken out of service with visible damage to the right wingtip. No request was issued for a return to field as I felt in the short time frame; and with how busy the crew would have been setting up an unexpected approach; that it would have been unsafe to add more to their workload. Operations staff need to be fully aware of their limitations in regards to operational control of flights. Perhaps there needs to be a rapid communication procedure for the ground personnel; as they had to make several calls to get the information to someone who could have made a difference quicker.
column123: After we took off and checked on with ZZZ Departure Control we were advised by the controller that Company wanted us to return to the airport. Upon questioning; the controller did not know the reason. I sent an ACARS message to our Dispatcher advising of an air turn back and asked why. His response was that he didn't know but would find out. We set up for the return to ZZZ and landed uneventfully and taxied to parking. Upon aircraft shutdown and secure a ZZZ maintenance representative met us inside the cockpit to advise us that the right wingtip possibly came into contact with a set of crew stairs during block out. We took a look at the wing and there was some minor damage to the right outboard leading edge slat just inside the right navigation light. At all times during the block out we were under the guidance and direction of the marshaller. Appropriate logbook entry made and reports submitted by both myself and First Officer. Reflecting upon blocking out; after engine start we cleared the mechanic and ascertained immediate area left and right were clear; I signaled the marshaller across the ramp and on the nose that we were ready to taxi out. We were marshaled straight out into the alley and given the signal for a left turn into the alley followed by a wave-off and salute. During the initial block out taxi roll; the First Officer mentioned the crew stairs seemed close; but from my position the stairs did not appear to be encroaching on the taxi lane and I continued to follow the marshaller's instructions. All marshaling signals were consistent with the aircraft being clear of any obstacles; and at no time did the marshaller give us a stop signal during the taxi out; nor did we feel any bump from the right wingtip possibly making contact with the crew stairs. I do not know if there was a wing-walker on the right wing due proximity of ground equipment between our aircraft and the aircraft to our right. I do recall a white ramp vehicle was encroached in the clear area to our right as we were blocking out; but the vehicle backed up out of the way. Recommendations: wing-walkers; all ground equipment clear; equipment safe boxes painted on the ground around the aircraft like in ZZZ1.

column121: The airplane was released with Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) deferred; thus required air-cart start procedures in the gate.  Preflight; airplane setup; briefings; checklists; crew duties; paperwork; ground interactions were all normal; and (Minimum Equipment Lists) MELs were complied with.  Normal air-cart start and subsequent pushback were all normal.  After clearing the ground crew off the headset; the Right; Number 1 Inner Tank Fuel Pump faulted.  We complied with the instruction to turn off the pump; and contacted Ramp Control and Maintenance on separate radios.The Captain worked with Maintenance while the First Officer worked with Ramp Control.   The Captain discussed the need to do a deferral and the First Officer received instructions for us to taxi to spot for off the gate maintenance; or something to that effect.  Neither of us had ever heard of such a thing; and I told the First Officer to say; 'No; we're not doing that.'I called on my cell phone and told them about the situation; and we began discussing the need for a maintenance deferral; and whether or not we had enough fuel under the circumstances.  I suggested we look at deleting the alternate from the flight plan if it would be legal to do so.  The Dispatcher said he'd begin working on it.  It was about this time that Maintenance suggested we go to a designated spot for hot refueling.  I again said we wouldn't do that and that the best plan should we need fuel would be to just taxi into the gate we just left; shut down; get fuel; and have Maintenance sign off the fuel pump.  Maintenance told me that that wasn't the best idea because if we did that we'd have a long delay and have to do the paperwork over again.  I called Dispatch back and he said there was no way we could just do the deferral and that we'd need to go back for fuel; and I said fine we will do that.  As a note; Dispatch told me that he had also never heard of hot refueling. At that point I told Maintenance what we were going to go back into the gate.  Maintenance proceeded to explain that the hot refuel was done all the time and that the FAA and that Company Safety had approved of the procedure.  He was adamant that the hot fuel was the best way to proceed.  Ramp also confirmed the procedure; so after discussing it as a crew; we agreed it sounded like a legitimate request; and we agreed to go to the spot and proceed with the fueling there.  When we arrived; we were stopped by a pickup truck pulling close to the airplane that made me stop.  There was no further guidance from Ramp; other than to ask us to pull the tail clear of a taxi lane.  A second vehicle with built-in airstairs arrived at the airplane.  He began giving us hand signals that made little sense; and eventually hooked up to the intercom system; and asked us to shut down the engines.  I suggested that was not a very good idea and that we could have done that in the gate and that we were there for hot fueling.  He then said to just shut down engine number two and to open the door so he could give us a fuel slip.  I asked the First Officer to do an after landing flow to make sure we were caught up; and then to open the door after disarming the slides.We received fuel; a fuel slip; coordinated hand signals; ran appropriate checklists; did a cross-bleed start to get engine number two back on line; accomplished the after-start checklist; and taxied via Ramp's instructions.  The First Officer made adjustments to the aircraft performance data and we ran a new performance briefing; noting a two knot increase in the new V speeds; and feeling comfortable that we had returned to safely normal operations. We proceeded to taxi and takeoff with normal operations.At cruise we received a message from Dispatch that we didn't do a new weight and balance.  He asked for our fuel onboard; we sent them. Either an ill conceived procedure or a lack of adequate resources for flight crews to safely conduct this procedure.The Pilot in Command shouldhave stuck to his first decision.  And from a more proactive approach; a checklist should be developed and added to the QRH.  The maintenance deferral flowchart should mention the need to revisit weight and balance. requirements and anything else we might have missed.  Additionally; I would highly encourage a module during simulator training that runs crews through this exercise and the use of new flow charts and a checklist.
column123: The flight blocked out and then had a maintenance problem.  Right Inner Tank Inoperative. This not a flagged item; so the decision was made to put the aircraft in a maintenance area on the ramp. The Minimum Equipment List (MEL) requires 8800 lb penalty fuel and adjust fuel for FL200. Fueling is allowed in the maintenance area.  Since it was not a block turnback; a new release was not required. We did the prescribed procedure with Maintenance and I then sent a mini flight plan showing the new numbers with fuel penalties. After fueling was finished; I sent an ACARS asking for the new fuel breakdown so the hub could send a new Weight and Balance. However; the plane had already blocked and departed without an up to date to the weight and balance. I informed the Duty Officer and then tried to send the new weight and balance. The new weight and balance never showed up in the crew's ACARS messages although it showed up in the playback screen in ACARS. So I copied and pasted and sent the information; but did not notice that the information in the weight and balance that the hub sent was the information from the original block out. Even though we had received the correct fuel breakdown from the crew enroute.  The flight landed at its destination and I talked with the crew and passed them on to the Duty Officer. The initial problem was caused by crew departing without an updated weight and balance. I suggest following procedures when an aircraft blocks back to a maintenance area

column121: Aircraft X. ARD had previous write-up about compressor stalls on #3 Engine. Maintenance said the morning crew rejected the takeoff for compressor stalls; we read the write-up and maintenance action in detail and discussed the issue. We identified this as a potential threat to our flight. On push back; while starting #1 Engine; we got ENG 1 FADEC ALTN alert; we referred to the QRH; it also identified 'action code' as SW. After engine start; the Captain said we could recycle the switch and asked if I was okay with that; I replied if he was okay; I was okay. We selected FADEC ALTN; then selected it again to the normal function; the alert went away. Later as we taxied out; I thought about the PDM process and not consulting maintenance; but the Captain's action corrected the alert to the proper configuration without any alerts and without an AML write-up; so I resolved my dilemma internally. Prior to taking the runway; the Captain announced he was gonna run-up all the engines a bit higher than usual while holding the brakes to ensure #3 Engine was operating correctly; I replied it was a good idea. It was my take-off (hand flown as briefed) and everything went normal up to about 700 ft. AGL.About 700 ft. AGL; with the gear up and flaps extended; we heard loud bangs associated with a compressor stall (I only heard this before in the sim) and a jolting in the plane; there were no differing indications on any of the engine instruments (all three N1; EGT; and N2 indications were identical). Around 1;000 ft. AGL; the Captain said he was gonna shut the engine down; I said okay with the bias of the previous write-up in the ARD; also thinking we'd go thru the process of 'Throttle-Idle; Fuel Shutoff Switch-Off' (I admit this wasn't the calm and rehearsed engine failure problem in the sim; and I was a bit anxious about the actual compressor stall). About that time; Tower called us and said we had intermittent flames shooting out of the left side (#1 Engine); the Captain said 'left side; I shut down [Engine] #3' (paraphrase). I looked down and noticed 0 fuel flow and the engine N2 decreasing while the banging continued. I exclaimed 'Let's start it back up' thinking #3 wasn't the problem and we definitely needed it if we had to shut down #1! The Captain quickly returned the fuel cutoff switch to on and I saw the N2 increase. I turned the autopilot on (as briefed if we had a problem) and announced I was disconnecting the auto throttles while the Captain told Tower we were returning to the field for compressor stalls and advised ATC. Tower told us to turn left downwind for [Runway] XX and I told the Captain 'I got the plane and the radios' and I replied to Tower. With the autopilot on and above 1;000 ft. AGL; the plane accelerated above Vf and I asked Tower if 2;000 ft. MSL was okay to level off; Tower replied yes. As I started the heading guided turn to the left; I adjusted the altitude to 2;000 ft. and manually retarded all the throttles for level off then selected airspeed 200 knots. With the throttles out of take-off power; the banging went away; I believe Tower said the flames stopped. While flying downwind abeam the field; I began to setup for the approach [Runway] XX; adjusted the minimums (already had it preselected); and announced I was moving the flaps to 15 degrees since they were still extended. Tower asked if we had the field insight; I replied yes and Tower cleared us the visual approach [Runway] XX and cleared to land; I repeated the clearance but said we were gonna fly out a bit to get our normal visual glidepath. After the Captain programmed the FMS and inserted the ILS frequency into the NavRad page; I called for the approach check and turned base to final; on dogleg; I began the descent on glidepath before intercepting the localizer and called for the gear down and before landing check. With the final configuration and checklist complete; I asked the Captain if he wanted the landing since we were an emergency; he took control of the plane with the autopilot on while I briefed him of the FMAs. Landing was uneventful.  We taxied clear onto taxiway XX and waited for the fire truck's inspection. With the all clear (no fire); we terminated the emergency and taxied to parking.Engine compressor stall.Some missteps between the crew while successfully resolving an engine compressor stall. Better crew coordination would simplify resolution.
column123: Alerted that Aircraft X might be returning to ZZZ due to problem with #1 Engine. I immediately contacted ZZZ Tower. Flight returned to airport and landed without issue on Runway XX. I talked to the Captain. He said that right after takeoff; there was compressor stall #1 Engine. They advised ATC and returned to ZZZ. The aircraft was met by the Fire Department. The Captain said he did not know what caused the loss of the #1 Engine. He also said the maintenance told him there was damage to the engine.
